newsitem.title: GERMANY: No coalition deal on cutting German solidarity tax.
newsitem.headline: No coalition deal on cutting German solidarity tax.

text.p: Leaders from Chancellor Helmut Kohl's three-party coalition government failed again to agree on when and by how much a tax raised to aid east Germany should be cut, coalition sources said on Tuesday.

Cutting the solidarity surcharge has become a sore point between the Free Democrats (FDP), staking their political fate on tax cuts, and Kohl's Christian Democrats (CDU) keen to bolster state revenues ahead of European monetary union.

The FDP, junior partners in Kohl's 14-year government, want a two-point cut in the 7.5 percent solidarity surcharge in 1998 after a revenue crunch this autumn forced it to abandon hard-won concesssions for a one-point cut next year.

But the sources said Finance Minister Theo Waigel got no answers from the FDP at a meeting on Monday night to his call for ideas on how to finance the 16 billion mark shortfall in revenues that would result from the cut.
More talks are planned on Wednesday. Both the Christian Democrat wing of the coalition and the FDP said they still wanted a deal before Christmas.
The FDP wants the solidarity surcharge, brought in after unification to help rebuild east Germany's battered economy, to be cut in the lead-up to a major overhaul of the tax system.
